items.prompt: What does TLS actually encrypt?
choices: The connection between a browser and a server, so eavesdroppers see scrambled bytes instead of readable data
The contents of the site's entire database as it's stored on the server's physical disk
The user's entire computer's hard drive, including every unrelated file stored on it
Only the password field inside a login form, leaving every other field fully visible
items.reference:
🔐 TLS — encrypts the connection in transit
🚫 Says nothing about who's on the other end
items.explanation: TLS encrypts the connection between browser and server in transit — so a network eavesdropper sees scrambled bytes instead of readable data. It's a guarantee about the pipe, not about who's on the other end of it.

items.prompt: Why does this unit describe TLS's guarantee as being "about the pipe, not about who's on the other end"?
choices: Because TLS encrypts traffic in transit but doesn't verify the trustworthiness of the destination's content or intent
Because TLS, as a protocol, doesn't actually encrypt anything meaningful at all
Because TLS, as a protocol, only ever actually works for email traffic, not web traffic
Because the word 'pipe' here refers to a literal physical cable that TLS directly protects
items.reference:
🔐 TLS — encrypts the connection in transit
🚫 Says nothing about who's on the other end
items.explanation: The "pipe" metaphor captures that TLS secures the data in transit between two endpoints — it makes no claim about whether the destination endpoint is trustworthy, honest, or who it claims to be.

items.prompt: How does this unit define a "certificate"?
choices: A simple password that's stored directly on the web server itself
A signed document binding a public key to a domain name, issued by a certificate authority
A complete list of every single user who has ever visited that particular site
A backup copy of the website's entire source code, kept for disaster recovery
items.reference:
📜 Certificate — binds a public key to a domain name
✍️ Signed by a certificate authority
items.explanation: A certificate is a signed document that binds a public key to a specific domain name — signed by a certificate authority whose signature browsers already trust.

items.prompt: What two things does a certificate bind together?
choices: A username and a password
A public key and a domain name
A browser version and an operating system
An IP address and a MAC address
items.reference:
📜 Certificate — binds a public key to a domain name
✍️ Signed by a certificate authority
items.explanation: A certificate binds a public key to a domain name — this binding, signed by a trusted CA, is what lets a browser confirm it's encrypting traffic to the party that controls that specific domain.

items.prompt: What is a "certificate authority (CA)"?
choices: A government agency that formally regulates all internet traffic worldwide
An organization whose signing key is pre-trusted by browsers and operating systems, forming the basis of the chain of trust
Any website at all that has simply purchased its own domain name
A browser extension whose main job is to block unwanted advertisements
items.reference:
🏛️ CA — signing key pre-trusted by browsers/OSes
🔗 A cert is trusted if it chains back to one
items.explanation: A certificate authority is an organization whose signing key browsers and operating systems already trust in advance — a certificate is considered trusted if its signature chain leads back to one of these.

items.prompt: Why does a certificate need to chain back to a CA's key rather than just being self-declared by the website?
choices: Because the CA's key is pre-trusted by browsers, so the chain of signatures gives the browser a reason to trust the certificate without knowing the website in advance
Self-declared certificates are actually just as trustworthy in practice, this is only a bureaucratic formality
Because CAs charge a fee for every certificate they issue, and this unit claims that fee is the only real reason anyone trusts them
Because browsers are technically incapable of processing a self-declared certificate at all
items.reference:
🏛️ CA — signing key pre-trusted by browsers/OSes
🔗 A cert is trusted if it chains back to one
items.explanation: The whole point of the CA system is that browsers pre-trust a known, limited set of CA keys — a certificate signed by (or chaining to) one of those keys inherits that pre-existing trust, which a self-declared certificate with no such chain wouldn't have.

items.prompt: What is the "chain of trust", per this unit?
choices: A complete list of every single website a given user has ever visited in their browser
The sequence of signatures from a leaf certificate up through intermediate certificates to a trusted root CA
A fallback mechanism used specifically for recovering a forgotten account password
The literal physical cable route that the underlying network data actually travels through
items.reference:
🔗 Leaf → Intermediate → Root
✅ Each link verified by a signature
items.explanation: The chain of trust is the sequence of signatures connecting a site's own (leaf) certificate through one or more intermediate certificates up to a root CA the browser already trusts.

items.prompt: In a typical chain of trust, what signs the leaf certificate?
choices: The website's own server, which simply self-signs its own leaf certificate directly
An intermediate CA certificate, which in turn is signed by a root CA
The end user's browser
Nothing at all signs the leaf certificate — it's issued without any signature whatsoever
items.reference:
🔗 Leaf → Intermediate → Root
✅ Each link verified by a signature
items.explanation: In a typical chain, the leaf certificate is signed by an intermediate CA's certificate, which is itself signed by a root CA's key — a browser walks this chain, verifying each signature, until it reaches a root it already trusts.

items.prompt: What does "domain validation (DV)" confirm, per this unit?
choices: The requester's full legal identity along with their formal business registration details
Only that the requester controls the domain — not who they are or what they intend to use it for
That the domain in question has been actively in use for at least 10 continuous years
That the resulting site has no security vulnerabilities present anywhere in its code
items.reference:
⚡ DV — fastest, most common certificate type
✅ Confirms domain control only, not identity
items.explanation: Domain validation confirms only that the requester controls the domain in question — it says nothing about who the requester is, what organization they represent, or their intentions for the site.

items.prompt: Domain validation is described as "the most common, lightest-weight kind of certificate." What does "lightest-weight" mean here?
choices: The resulting certificate file itself is physically smaller in bytes than other certificate types
It requires the least amount of verification — just proving domain control, without deeper identity checks
It's a certificate type that, by design, only actually works on mobile devices
It expires faster than any other certificate type
items.reference:
⚡ DV — fastest, most common certificate type
✅ Confirms domain control only, not identity
items.explanation: "Lightest-weight" refers to the depth of verification required — DV certificates need only proof of domain control, which is why they can be issued quickly and automatically, unlike certificate types that also verify organizational identity.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what made the phishing site convincing enough that the user's padlock check didn't catch it?
choices: The phishing site actually had no TLS certificate at all, but the browser displayed a padlock anyway due to a rendering bug
The phishing site had a genuinely valid TLS certificate and a genuine padlock — the padlock's check passed truthfully
The victim had specifically disabled all security warnings inside their own browser's settings beforehand
The phishing site happened to be hosted on the exact same physical server as the real PayPal
items.reference:
🔒 paypal.com — valid cert, padlock shown
🔒 paypa1-secure-login.com — ALSO valid, ALSO padlock shown
items.explanation: The phishing site genuinely had a valid certificate and a genuine padlock — the padlock check passed truthfully because it only verifies domain control and encryption, neither of which the phishing site was lacking.

items.prompt: What was the actual domain of the phishing site in the opening scenario?
choices: paypal.com
paypa1-secure-login.com
secure.paypal.com
The scenario doesn't specify a domain
items.reference:
🔒 paypal.com — valid cert, padlock shown
🔒 paypa1-secure-login.com — ALSO valid, ALSO padlock shown
items.explanation: The phishing domain was `paypa1-secure-login.com` — a lookalike domain using the numeral "1" in place of the letter "l", designed to visually resemble a legitimate PayPal domain.

items.prompt: Per the unit's own answer to its opening question, what did the padlock actually promise in the phishing scenario?
choices: That the site was genuinely operated by the real, official PayPal company itself
That the connection to whatever domain was in the address bar was encrypted, and a CA verified someone controls that domain
That the site had already passed a formal, independent manual security audit
Nothing — the padlock is purely decorative and checks nothing
items.reference:
🔒 paypal.com — valid cert, padlock shown
🔒 paypa1-secure-login.com — ALSO valid, ALSO padlock shown
items.explanation: The unit's answer is precise: the padlock promises the connection to the domain in the address bar is encrypted and that a CA verified control of that exact domain — nothing about who that domain actually belongs to in the real world.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, how many checks does the browser perform before showing a padlock, and what are they?
choices: Three checks: a domain match, signature validity, and an added manual human review step
Two checks: does the certificate's domain match the address bar, and does every signature in the chain verify up to a trusted root
Just one single check: whether the site has ever previously been reported as malicious
Zero checks — the padlock appears automatically for any HTTPS site
items.reference:
1️⃣ Domain in cert matches address bar?
2️⃣ Every signature in the chain valid up to a trusted root?
items.explanation: L2's flowchart shows exactly two checks: whether the certificate's domain matches the address bar, and whether every signature in the chain verifies up to a trusted root — no human review, no deeper identity check, for the common case.

items.prompt: L2 states neither of the browser's two checks asks a certain question. What is it?
choices: "Is this organization who it claims to be" in any deeper sense than "do they control this specific domain name"
Simply "is the connection encrypted at all between the browser and the server"
"Does the certificate exist"
"Is the domain name spelled correctly according to an actual dictionary word list"
items.reference:
1️⃣ Domain in cert matches address bar?
2️⃣ Every signature in the chain valid up to a trusted root?
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that neither check asks "is this organization who it claims to be" beyond domain control — that deeper identity question is simply out of scope for the standard chain-of-trust verification most sites use.

items.prompt: Per L2's two-column table, which of these is something the padlock DOES prove?
choices: The site's content is honest and non-malicious
The certificate's domain matches the address bar exactly
The domain is operated by the company the user assumes
The server won't misuse data once it arrives
items.reference:
PROVESencrypted in transit; domain matches address bar; CA verified domain control
DOESN'T PROVEcontent is honest; domain is who you think; real-world identity vetted; server won't misuse data
items.explanation: L2's left column (what the padlock proves) includes exact domain matching to the address bar — one of only a few things the padlock actually guarantees, distinct from the much larger list of things it does not guarantee.

items.prompt: Per L2's two-column table, which of these is something the padlock does NOT prove?
choices: That the connection is encrypted in transit
That data can't be silently read by a network eavesdropper
That the domain is operated by the company or person the user assumes
That a trusted certificate authority verified control of that domain
items.reference:
PROVESencrypted in transit; domain matches address bar; CA verified domain control
DOESN'T PROVEcontent is honest; domain is who you think; real-world identity vetted; server won't misuse data
items.explanation: "The domain is operated by the company or person the user assumes" sits firmly in the right column — the padlock never verifies real-world ownership or brand identity, only domain control and encryption.

items.prompt: L2 says "the gap between these two columns is exactly where phishing over HTTPS lives." What does this mean?
choices: Phishing sites can satisfy everything in the "proves" column while still doing real harm through the "doesn't prove" column
Phishing becomes entirely impossible once a site has obtained a genuinely valid TLS certificate
The two columns actually describe exactly the same set of guarantees, so there's no real gap between them
Phishing sites can never obtain a valid TLS certificate under any circumstances
items.reference:
PROVESencrypted in transit; domain matches address bar; CA verified domain control
DOESN'T PROVEcontent is honest; domain is who you think; real-world identity vetted; server won't misuse data
items.explanation: L2's point is that a phishing site can legitimately satisfy every item the padlock actually verifies (encryption, domain match, CA-verified control) while still causing real harm through everything the padlock never claimed to check — that's the exploited gap.

items.prompt: L2 explains why domain validation was "deliberately designed to be lightweight." What was the reasoning?
choices: Because certificate authorities are legally forbidden by regulation from performing any deeper identity checks
Because fast, automated, cheap issuance is what made HTTPS practical for the entire web to adopt at scale
Because lightweight domain checks are, counterintuitively, actually more secure than thorough identity checks
Because it was an accident of early internet design with no deliberate reasoning
items.reference:
⚡ DV: automated, minutes, no human review
🏢 EV: adds real identity checks, but rare and no longer visually distinguished
items.explanation: L2 explains that DV's speed and automation is what let HTTPS scale to the entire web — a certificate issued within minutes with no human review, trading deeper identity verification for practicality at massive scale.

items.prompt: What does L2 say about Extended Validation (EV) certificates today?
choices: They are, today, by far the most common certificate type issued across the entire web
They add real organizational identity checks but are far less common, and browsers no longer visually distinguish them from DV certificates the way they used to
They've been completely banned outright by every major browser vendor in recent years
They require no verification at all to obtain, completely unlike domain-validated certificates which still check domain control
items.reference:
⚡ DV: automated, minutes, no human review
🏢 EV: adds real identity checks, but rare and no longer visually distinguished
items.explanation: L2 notes that EV certificates do add genuine organizational identity verification, but they're far less common than DV certificates, and modern browsers no longer show a distinct visual indicator for them — so most users never see the difference even when it exists.

items.prompt: L2 lists "treating HTTPS as a synonym for trustworthy" as a failure mode. What's the correct distinction?
choices: HTTPS answers "is this connection private," not "should I trust what's on the other end"
HTTPS and trustworthiness are actually the exact same thing, so this isn't really a failure mode
HTTPS has nothing to do with privacy at all
HTTPS only applies to banking websites specifically
items.reference:
⚠️ HTTPS = private connection, not vetted destination
⚠️ Most certs are domain-only, not identity-vetted
items.explanation: L2's correction is that HTTPS answers a narrow question — is this connection private — and conflating that with "should I trust the destination" is exactly the confusion phishing over HTTPS exploits.

items.prompt: Why does L2 warn against assuming a CA vetted an organization's real-world identity?
choices: Because for the overwhelming majority of certificates (domain-validated), the CA only checked domain control, not a business registration or physical address
Because certificate authorities never actually verify anything at all, for any certificate type whatsoever
Because every single certificate issued legally requires full government ID verification of the requester
Because this particular trust concern doesn't actually apply to any real certificates issued in practice today
items.reference:
⚠️ HTTPS = private connection, not vetted destination
⚠️ Most certs are domain-only, not identity-vetted
items.explanation: For the vast majority of certificates in use (domain-validated), the CA verified only domain control — not a business registration, physical address, or who's actually operating the site, which is exactly the assumption L2 warns against making.

items.prompt: In L3's `signCert`/`verifyCertSignature` implementation, what cryptographic algorithm is used?
choices: A simple raw string comparison between values, with no real cryptography involved at all
SHA-256 hashing combined with RSA signing/verification via Node's built-in `crypto` module
A custom, hand-rolled encryption algorithm written specifically for this unit's example code
Base64 encoding, which L3 treats as equivalent to encryption
items.reference:
1️⃣ leafCert.subject === hostname
2️⃣ intermediateCert signed by rootPublicKey
3️⃣ leafCert signed by intermediateCert.publicKey
items.explanation: L3 uses Node's built-in `crypto` module for genuine SHA-256/RSA signing and verification — `crypto.sign("sha256", ...)` and `crypto.verify("sha256", ...)` — not a toy stand-in, so the verification result reflects real cryptographic behavior.

items.prompt: In L3's `verifyChain` function, what are the exact three checks performed, in order?
choices: Check the certificate's reported file size, check its expiration date, and check the issuer's listed country
Hostname matches leaf subject; intermediate is signed by the trusted root; leaf is signed by the intermediate
Only one check: whether the domain has ever been reported as malicious
Check that the site uses HTTPS, check that it shows a green padlock, and check that the page loads quickly
items.reference:
1️⃣ leafCert.subject === hostname
2️⃣ intermediateCert signed by rootPublicKey
3️⃣ leafCert signed by intermediateCert.publicKey
items.explanation: L3's `verifyChain` performs exactly three checks in order: hostname match against the leaf's subject, the intermediate's signature verified against the trusted root's public key, and the leaf's signature verified against the intermediate's public key.

items.prompt: What is HTTPS, per this unit?
choices: A completely separate protocol from HTTP with no relationship to it
HTTP running over TLS
A faster version of HTTP with no encryption involved
A protocol used only for file downloads, never for regular web browsing
items.reference:
🌐 HTTPS = HTTP + TLS
🔐 TLS supplies the encryption layer underneath
items.explanation: HTTPS is simply HTTP running over TLS — the same HTTP requests and responses, but wrapped in the encrypted, authenticated connection TLS provides.

items.prompt: Why does defining HTTPS as "HTTP over TLS" matter for understanding what a padlock guarantees?
choices: It doesn't matter at all — HTTPS and TLS are, conceptually, completely unrelated to each other
It clarifies that the padlock reflects TLS's guarantees specifically (encryption, domain-bound certificate) layered under ordinary HTTP, not some separate, broader safety system
It means HTTPS requires an entirely different, incompatible set of HTML tags compared to plain HTTP
It means that HTTPS sites, by definition, always load their content roughly twice as fast as equivalent HTTP sites
items.reference:
🌐 HTTPS = HTTP + TLS
🔐 TLS supplies the encryption layer underneath
items.explanation: Understanding HTTPS as HTTP layered over TLS clarifies that the padlock reflects exactly TLS's specific guarantees (encryption, domain-bound certificate verification) — not some separate, broader safety or trustworthiness system with its own independent checks.

items.prompt: L2 says the domain-match check is "strict about the exact string in the address bar." What does this mean in practice?
choices: The check deliberately ignores minor spelling differences between two visually similar-looking domains
A certificate for `paypal.com` will not satisfy a domain-match check for `paypa1-secure-login.com`, or vice versa — the strings must match exactly (or match a wildcard pattern)
The check only actually bothers to compare the very first letter of each domain string
The domain-match check described here doesn't actually exist at all and was simply invented for this unit's example
items.reference:
🔍 Domain-match check: exact string, no fuzzy matching
🙋 But it can't tell a human that a lookalike string isn't the real brand
items.explanation: The domain-match check is strict and exact — a certificate issued for one exact domain string won't satisfy a check against a different string, even a visually similar one. What it can't do is judge whether a *different, valid* domain string is a legitimate brand's domain or a deliberate lookalike.

items.prompt: L2 notes the domain-match check "can't tell a human that paypa1-secure-login.com isn't paypal.com." Why not, given that the check is exact and strict?
choices: Because the check only verifies that the certificate's domain matches whatever is in the address bar — it has no concept of which domains are legitimate brands versus lookalikes
Because the underlying check is actually broken and fails to verify anything correctly at all
Because `paypa1-secure-login.com` and `paypal.com` are, strictly speaking, technically treated as the exact same string by a computer performing the comparison
Because browsers, in practice, don't actually perform this particular check at all
items.reference:
🔍 Domain-match check: exact string, no fuzzy matching
🙋 But it can't tell a human that a lookalike string isn't the real brand
items.explanation: The check verifies certificate-to-address-bar string matching only — it has no notion of "legitimate brand" versus "lookalike domain," so a completely valid, correctly-matching certificate for a phishing domain passes the check just as truthfully as one for the real brand would.

items.prompt: In L3's CA hierarchy setup, how many separate RSA key pairs are generated in total?
choices: Two — one for the root, one shared by everything else
Four — root, intermediate, the legitimate leaf, and the phishing leaf
One single key pair used for the entire chain
L3 doesn't generate any real key pairs, only mock placeholders
items.reference:
🔑 root, intermediate, leafLegit, leafPhish — 4 real key pairs
🏛️ Same intermediate CA signs both leaf certs
items.explanation: L3 generates four separate RSA key pairs: `root`, `intermediate`, `leafLegit`, and `leafPhish` — each a genuine key pair produced by `crypto.generateKeyPairSync`.

items.prompt: In L3's setup, which entity signs both the legitimate `paypal.com` leaf certificate and the phishing `paypa1-secure-login.com` leaf certificate?
choices: Two completely different, unrelated intermediate CAs
The exact same intermediate CA signs both
The root CA signs the leaves directly, skipping the intermediate entirely
Neither certificate is actually signed by anything in L3's example
items.reference:
🔑 root, intermediate, leafLegit, leafPhish — 4 real key pairs
🏛️ Same intermediate CA signs both leaf certs
items.explanation: The same intermediate CA signs both the legitimate and phishing leaf certificates in L3's example — reinforcing that a single CA has no built-in way to distinguish a brand's real domain from a lookalike domain, since both requesters equally proved control of their respective domains.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the CA have "no way to know, and no obligation to check" that one domain is impersonating a well-known brand?
choices: Because the CA only verifies domain control for each requester, and both `paypal.com` and `paypa1-secure-login.com` requesters could each prove control of their own distinct domain
Because certificate authorities are legally required by international law to ignore brand impersonation entirely
Because the particular CA's issuance software has a known bug that always approves every single request
Because this unit's L3 content explicitly claims that CAs never, in practice, issue certificates to phishing domains
items.reference:
🔑 root, intermediate, leafLegit, leafPhish — 4 real key pairs
🏛️ Same intermediate CA signs both leaf certs
items.explanation: L3 explains that domain validation only checks control of the specific domain being requested — since `paypa1-secure-login.com` is a distinct, real domain that its requester genuinely controlled, the CA has no cryptographic basis to distinguish it from any other legitimately-controlled domain, brand impersonation or not.

items.prompt: Before writing `verifyChain`, what question should you expect it to answer?
choices: Does this certificate chain to a trusted root for the exact hostname in the address bar?
Is this particular site honest, and genuinely safe to type a password into right now?
Does this company actually own the real brand that this domain's name merely resembles?
Will this page avoid all phishing and malware?
items.explanation: `verifyChain` answers a narrow technical question about domain-to-key binding. It does not judge brand identity or intent.
items.reference:
Function contract vs user judgment
Chain verification answers domain binding. The user or a separate anti-phishing system still checks whether the domain is the intended brand.

items.prompt: You see a padlock on `paypa1-secure-login.com`. What should you still check before entering a password?
choices: Whether the domain text is the real domain you intended to visit, not just a lookalike with one changed character
Whether the padlock icon shown in the address bar appears sufficiently green in color
Whether the page loads quickly
Whether the password entry box on the page is neatly centered in the browser window
items.explanation: The padlock can be valid for the lookalike domain. The human still has to notice that `paypa1` is not `paypal`.
items.reference:
Function contract vs user judgment
Chain verification answers domain binding. The user or a separate anti-phishing system still checks whether the domain is the intended brand.

items.prompt: Implement `verifyChain(leafCert, intermediateCert, trustedRootId, hostname)` using this simplified mock-signature model: each cert is `{ subject, issuer, signedBy }` where `signedBy` holds the id of whoever actually signed it. Return `{ valid: false, reason: 'hostname mismatch' }` if `leafCert.subject !== hostname`. Return `{ valid: false, reason: 'intermediate not signed by trusted root' }` if `intermediateCert.signedBy !== trustedRootId`. Return `{ valid: false, reason: 'leaf not signed by intermediate' }` if `leafCert.signedBy !== intermediateCert.subject`. Otherwise return `{ valid: true, reason: 'chain verifies to a trusted root, hostname matches' }`.

tests.expr: expect(verifyChain({ subject: 'paypal.com', issuer: 'IntermediateCA', signedBy: 'IntermediateCA' }, { subject: 'IntermediateCA', issuer: 'RootCA', signedBy: 'RootCA' }, 'RootCA', 'paypal.com').valid).toBe(true)

expect(verifyChain({ subject: 'paypal.com', issuer: 'IntermediateCA', signedBy: 'IntermediateCA' }, { subject: 'IntermediateCA', issuer: 'RootCA', signedBy: 'RootCA' }, 'RootCA', 'evil.com').reason).toBe('hostname mismatch')

tests.description: rejects an intermediate not signed by the trusted root
tests.expr: expect(verifyChain({ subject: 'paypal.com', issuer: 'IntermediateCA', signedBy: 'IntermediateCA' }, { subject: 'IntermediateCA', issuer: 'RootCA', signedBy: 'UntrustedRoot' }, 'RootCA', 'paypal.com').valid).toBe(false)

tests.description: rejects a leaf not signed by the intermediate
tests.expr: expect(verifyChain({ subject: 'paypal.com', issuer: 'IntermediateCA', signedBy: 'SomeOtherCA' }, { subject: 'IntermediateCA', issuer: 'RootCA', signedBy: 'RootCA' }, 'RootCA', 'paypal.com').valid).toBe(false)

tests.description: a phishing domain with a legitimately-signed chain still validates true
tests.expr: expect(verifyChain({ subject: 'paypa1-secure-login.com', issuer: 'IntermediateCA', signedBy: 'IntermediateCA' }, { subject: 'IntermediateCA', issuer: 'RootCA', signedBy: 'RootCA' }, 'RootCA', 'paypa1-secure-login.com').valid).toBe(true)

items.explanation: The last test is the important one: a phishing domain with a completely legitimate, correctly-signed certificate chain still returns `valid: true` — exactly matching L3's real crypto-based demonstration that chain verification succeeding says nothing about whether the domain belongs to who the user thinks it does.
items.reference:
1️⃣ leafCert.subject === hostname
2️⃣ intermediateCert signed by rootPublicKey
3️⃣ leafCert signed by intermediateCert.publicKey

items.prompt: Write `hostnameMatches(certSubject, addressBarHost)` that returns `true` if a certificate's subject matches the browser's address bar hostname. Support an exact match, and a leading wildcard (`*.example.com` matches `mail.example.com` but NOT `example.com` itself, and NOT `sub.mail.example.com` — a wildcard only covers exactly one extra label).

tests.description: wildcard does not match the bare domain
wildcard does not match two levels of subdomain

items.explanation: A wildcard certificate is scoped to exactly one label of subdomain — matching the label count keeps `*.example.com` from silently matching either the bare domain or a deeper nested subdomain, both of which would widen the certificate's actual scope beyond what it was issued for.
items.reference:
✅ Exact match: subject === hostname
⭐ Wildcard: matches exactly one extra label, not zero or two+

items.prompt: L3 verifies both `paypal.com` and `paypa1-secure-login.com`'s certificate chains. What does the result of running both checks show?
choices: Only the legitimate domain's chain verifies as valid; the phishing domain's chain fails
Both chains verify as `valid: true` — this is the correct, honest result, not a bug
Both chains fail to verify, since phishing domains can never obtain valid certificates
The verifier crashes when given the phishing domain's certificate
items.reference:
✅ Both chains verify true — correct, not a bug
❓ Neither the CA nor verifier was ever asked "is this the real PayPal"
items.explanation: Both chains verify as `valid: true` in L3's demonstration — this is explicitly not a bug in the verifier; it's the correct result for the question the verifier was actually built to answer (domain-to-key binding), which never included "is this the real PayPal."

items.prompt: Why does L3 insist that both chains validating true is "not a bug in the verifier"?
choices: Because the chain-of-trust verifier itself is simply broken and urgently needs to be rewritten
Because the chain-of-trust check answered exactly the question it's designed to answer — truthfully — for both domains; "is this the real PayPal" was never part of its contract
Because bugs of this particular kind are, as a category, genuinely impossible to occur in any cryptographic verification code
Because, in this particular example, the phishing domain was actually registered by PayPal itself
items.reference:
✅ Both chains verify true — correct, not a bug
❓ Neither the CA nor verifier was ever asked "is this the real PayPal"
items.explanation: L3 argues the verifier is functioning exactly as intended — it truthfully answers "does this certificate chain to a trusted root for this domain," and that question was correctly answered yes for both domains, since brand-identity verification was never part of what the function checks.

items.prompt: In L3's tampering test, what happens when `legitLeafCert`'s `subject` field is changed to `paypal.com-but-tampered` without re-signing?
choices: The signature still verifies successfully regardless, proving that tampering is fundamentally undetectable
The signature verification returns false, since the signature covers the exact original certificate contents
The tampered certificate automatically gets silently re-signed by the intermediate CA on the next check
Nothing happens — the tampering test isn't actually run in L3
items.reference:
🔨 Tampered subject, same old signature
❌ verifyCertSignature returns false — signature no longer matches contents
items.explanation: L3 shows that modifying `subject` without re-signing breaks verification — `verifyCertSignature` returns `false`, since the signature was computed over the original contents and no longer matches the altered payload.

items.prompt: What does the tampering test demonstrate about the limits of what the verifier catches, per L3?
choices: That the verifier reliably catches every possible kind of certificate misuse, including lookalike domain names
That the verifier correctly detects post-issuance tampering, but detecting a lookalike domain string is a separate, non-cryptographic problem it was never built to solve
That tampering of this kind can genuinely never be detected by any cryptographic verification system
That the verifier, given this result, is completely useless overall and should simply be discarded entirely

🔨 Tampered subject, same old signature
❌ verifyCertSignature returns false — signature no longer matches contents
items.explanation: L3 uses the tampering test to show the verifier isn't useless — it correctly catches post-issuance tampering — while making clear that detecting a lookalike domain string is a fundamentally different, lexical (not cryptographic) problem that has to be solved elsewhere.

The unit itself doesn't actually ever answer this particular question anywhere in its content

🔍 Lookalike-domain detection needs a separate, deliberate check
items.explanation: L3 explicitly rejects "TLS is pointless" — the encryption and hostname-match guarantees remain real and valuable, since without them even the legitimate `paypal.com` would be vulnerable to network-level eavesdropping or tampering.

items.prompt: A certificate only contains a public key, and a public key alone is too slow to encrypt an entire page load. What closes that gap?
choices: The TLS handshake, which negotiates a cipher suite and derives a shared symmetric key before any page data moves
The browser simply reuses the exact same symmetric key for every single website it ever visits
The server emails the newly generated symmetric key over to the browser as a separate message
HTTPS skips encrypting the first page load entirely
items.reference:
🤝 Handshake — negotiates a cipher suite and a shared key
📜 Uses the certificate to authenticate that negotiation
items.explanation: The TLS handshake is the short negotiation that happens before any page data moves: the two sides agree on a cipher suite and derive a shared symmetric key, using the server's certificate to authenticate that negotiation so an eavesdropper can't hijack it.

items.prompt: What does this unit call the short negotiation, before any page data moves, where client and server agree on a cipher suite and a shared key?
choices: The TLS handshake
The chain of trust
Domain validation
The certificate revocation check
items.reference:
🤝 Handshake — negotiates a cipher suite and a shared key
📜 Uses the certificate to authenticate that negotiation
items.explanation: That negotiation is the TLS handshake — distinct from the chain-of-trust check, which verifies the certificate itself rather than negotiating the key used afterward.

items.prompt: What is a "cipher suite", per this unit?
choices: The agreed bundle of algorithms (key exchange, encryption, and integrity check) a connection will use
A complete historical list of every single cipher algorithm ever invented by cryptographers
The certificate authority's own private, internal signing key used to issue certificates
A backup encryption key stored by the browser vendor
items.reference:
🧩 Cipher suite — key exchange + encryption + integrity check, bundled
🔄 Negotiated fresh so algorithms can be retired without breaking everyone
items.explanation: A cipher suite names the specific bundle of algorithms a connection will use: which key-exchange method, which symmetric cipher for the traffic itself, and which integrity check detects tampering.

items.prompt: Why do client and server negotiate a cipher suite instead of every TLS connection always using one fixed, hard-coded algorithm?
choices: So TLS can keep working as old algorithms are found weak and new ones replace them, without breaking clients and servers that haven't upgraded yet
Negotiation of this kind is purely decorative in practice and has no real effect on the resulting connection
Because only certificates that were paid for are legally allowed to pick their own cipher suite
Because browsers are legally required to offer a choice
items.reference:
🧩 Cipher suite — key exchange + encryption + integrity check, bundled
🔄 Negotiated fresh so algorithms can be retired without breaking everyone
items.explanation: Negotiating a cipher suite lets both sides offer the strongest set of algorithms they each support and agree on the best match both understand — which is what lets TLS evolve (retiring weak algorithms, adopting new ones) without breaking everyone who hasn't upgraded yet.

items.prompt: What does "forward secrecy" mean, as this unit defines it?
choices: Even if the server's long-term private key leaks later, past sessions encrypted with an ephemeral key from that time can't be decrypted retroactively
The ability for a server to forward already-encrypted traffic to a backup server if the primary one fails
A guarantee that certificates never expire
A property that lets any browser decrypt traffic belonging to any website, not just the current one
items.reference:
⏳ Ephemeral key — generated per-session, discarded after
🔒 Stealing the long-term key later decrypts nothing already exchanged
items.explanation: Forward secrecy means that compromising the server's long-term private key at some point in the future tells an attacker nothing about a shared key from a past session, because that session's shared secret was derived from an ephemeral value that no longer exists anywhere.

items.prompt: An attacker steals a server's long-term certificate private key today. Under forward secrecy, what can they do with a recording of a handshake from last year that used an ephemeral ECDHE key exchange?
choices: Nothing — the ephemeral key-exchange values from that handshake were discarded after it ended and never depended on today's stolen key
They can immediately decrypt every single byte of that entire recorded session right away
They can decrypt it, but only if they also separately manage to steal the client's physical device
They can decrypt it, but only the first message of the session
items.reference:
⏳ Ephemeral key — generated per-session, discarded after
🔒 Stealing the long-term key later decrypts nothing already exchanged
items.explanation: Because the shared secret from an ECDHE handshake was derived from ephemeral values generated fresh for that one session and discarded immediately after, stealing the long-term private key later has nothing left to apply itself to — the actual secret-deriving values simply don't exist anywhere anymore.

items.prompt: Why does plain RSA key exchange NOT provide forward secrecy, while ECDHE does?
choices: RSA key exchange encrypts the shared secret directly with the server's long-term public key, so anyone who later gets the matching long-term private key can decrypt a recorded session; ECDHE's shared secret is derived from ephemeral values that are discarded after the handshake
RSA key exchange is simply a weaker cipher overall, using meaningfully shorter key lengths than ECDHE typically does, which is really the whole story here
RSA key exchange doesn't actually involve a certificate at all in the process, so there's nothing left behind for anyone to later compromise or steal
ECDHE avoids forward-secrecy problems entirely simply by never encrypting anything over the connection in the first place, which isn't actually how any of this works
items.reference:
✅ ECDHE — fresh key pair per handshake → forward secrecy
❌ Plain RSA key exchange — secret encrypted with the long-term key → no forward secrecy
items.explanation: Plain RSA key exchange has the client encrypt its chosen secret directly with the server's long-term public key — decryptable forever by whoever holds the matching long-term private key. ECDHE instead has both sides generate fresh, ephemeral key pairs for that one handshake and derive the shared secret from those; the ephemeral private values are discarded right after, so there is nothing left for a later-stolen long-term key to unlock.

items.prompt: What is the key difference between the key-exchange value used in ECDHE versus the one used in plain RSA key exchange?
choices: ECDHE's key-exchange value is ephemeral (generated fresh per handshake, then discarded); RSA key exchange's value is encrypted directly under the server's permanent, reused long-term key
There is no real difference between the two at all; both provide exactly identical forward secrecy guarantees
ECDHE, despite its name, doesn't actually perform any kind of key exchange at all during the handshake
RSA key exchange always uses a meaningfully longer key than ECDHE, and that's the only difference that actually matters
items.reference:
✅ ECDHE — fresh key pair per handshake → forward secrecy
❌ Plain RSA key exchange — secret encrypted with the long-term key → no forward secrecy
items.explanation: The defining difference is lifespan: ECDHE's key-exchange material is ephemeral, existing only for one handshake, while RSA key exchange routes the shared secret through the server's long-term, reused private key — which is exactly the value an attacker could compromise long after the fact.

items.prompt: A passive network observer records an entire TLS handshake and the encrypted traffic that follows, without ever obtaining any private key. Which of these can they actually learn?
choices: The negotiated TLS version, the cipher suite, and the server's certificate chain — all sent before encryption begins
The full plaintext contents of every single request and response body exchanged on the connection
The shared symmetric key itself
Exactly which specific URL path and query string the client ended up requesting from the server
items.reference:
👁️ Visible: TLS version, cipher suite, certificate chain, hostname (SNI)
🚫 Hidden: request/response bodies, headers, the shared key itself
items.explanation: ClientHello, ServerHello, and the certificate chain are all sent before encryption starts, so a passive observer sees the negotiated version, cipher suite, and certificate chain in the clear. Request/response bodies, the path and query string, and the shared key itself are exactly what the subsequent encryption protects.

items.prompt: Why can a passive observer typically learn which hostname a client connected to over TLS, even though the request path and body stay encrypted?
choices: Because SNI (Server Name Indication), part of the ClientHello, sends the hostname in the clear so the server knows which certificate to present — unless Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is in use
Because the requested hostname is actually sent as part of the already-encrypted response body
Because TLS has no concept of hostnames at all
Because the server's full certificate chain is always deliberately withheld by the protocol until after the hostname itself has already been hidden from any observer
items.reference:
👁️ Visible: TLS version, cipher suite, certificate chain, hostname (SNI)
🚫 Hidden: request/response bodies, headers, the shared key itself
items.explanation: SNI is sent in the ClientHello, before encryption begins, precisely so a server hosting multiple domains on one IP knows which certificate to present — which means it's visible to a passive observer too, unless ECH is negotiated to encrypt that specific field.

items.prompt: Node's `tls` socket reports `getEphemeralKeyInfo()` as a populated object only when an ephemeral (ECDHE-style) key exchange was used, and as `undefined` for a connection that negotiated plain RSA key exchange. Write `hasForwardSecrecy(ephemeralKeyInfo)` that returns `true` when ephemeral key info was reported, and `false` when it's `undefined`.

tests.description: true for a real ECDHE ephemeralKeyInfo object
false when no ephemeral key info was reported (plain RSA key exchange)

items.explanation: Node only populates `ephemeralKeyInfo` when the negotiated key exchange actually generated ephemeral key material (ECDHE and its variants) — so its mere presence, not any specific field inside it, is the forward-secrecy signal. A connection that fell back to plain RSA key exchange has nothing ephemeral to report, hence `undefined`.
items.reference:
⏳ Ephemeral key — generated per-session, discarded after
🔒 Stealing the long-term key later decrypts nothing already exchanged

items.prompt: Write `countForwardSecretSessions(sessions)`, where `sessions` is an array of objects each shaped like `{ host, ephemeralKeyInfo }` (mirroring what `socket.getEphemeralKeyInfo()` would report per connection). Return the count of sessions whose `ephemeralKeyInfo` is a populated object (forward secrecy was provided), ignoring any session where it's `undefined` or `null`.

tests.description: counts only the sessions with populated ephemeralKeyInfo
tests.expr: expect(countForwardSecretSessions([{ host: 'a.com', ephemeralKeyInfo: { type: 'ECDH' } }, { host: 'b.com', ephemeralKeyInfo: undefined }, { host: 'c.com', ephemeralKeyInfo: { type: 'ECDH' } }])).toBe(2)

tests.description: returns 0 when no session has forward secrecy
tests.expr: expect(countForwardSecretSessions([{ host: 'a.com', ephemeralKeyInfo: undefined }, { host: 'b.com', ephemeralKeyInfo: null }])).toBe(0)

items.explanation: This is the same forward-secrecy signal as a single connection — a populated `ephemeralKeyInfo` — applied across a batch, which is exactly the kind of check a fleet-wide TLS configuration audit would run to find servers still falling back to non-ephemeral key exchange.
